title: A Helping Hand Before a Moral Lecture — Darwin’s (1871) Social Instincts, Warneken & Tomasello’s (2006/2007) Unrewarded Toddler & Chimpanzee Instrumental Helping & Hamann’s (2011) Collaborative vs. Windfall Equal Sharing

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: Before children can recite moral rules—and without gold stars or snacks—18-month-old toddlers and chimpanzees spontaneously help an adult reach a dropped clothespin (Warneken & Tomasello 2006), while 3-year-olds split spoils equally right after pulling a rope *together* (Hamann 2011).
teenKit.whyItMatters: Comparing pre-verbal toddlers and great apes separates ancient evolutionary building blocks of instrumental helping from uniquely human norms of collaborative fairness.
keyTakeaways: Warneken & Tomasello (2006, 2007) tested 18-month-old human infants and human-raised chimpanzees across novel out-of-reach tasks (unlike passive-drop controls), finding spontaneous unrewarded helping in both species.
Overjustification experiments showed extrinsic material rewards can actually *undermine* toddlers' intrinsic motivation to help.

Hamann, Warneken, Greenberg & Tomasello (2011) revealed a sharp species divergence in sharing: after joint collaborative work, 3-year-old human peers corrected unequal 3:1 windfalls to 2:2 equal splits far more reliably than chimpanzees or solo-work controls.

vocab.meaning: Assisting another agent to achieve a concrete action goal (e.g., handing back an accidentally dropped object or opening a blocked cabinet).
Matched experiment where the experimenter deliberately throws the clothespin on the floor, confirming subjects track unmet goals rather than reflexively fetching objects.
Dividing jointly earned spoils 50:50 with a partner who pulled together, distinct from passive windfall generosity.

quiz.question: How did Warneken & Tomasello (2006) prove 18-month-old toddlers and chimpanzees weren't just retrieving objects automatically?
options: They paired each accidental unmet-goal trial with a matched control where the experimenter deliberately threw or pushed the object without trying to reach it
They paid toddlers five dollars per clothespin
quiz.explanation: Both toddlers and chimpanzees helped selectively when the experimenter was genuinely trying and failing to reach the goal, not when the same action happened intentionally without need.
